What is the inversion coefficient IC, and what ranges define weak, moderate and strong inversion?
column2: \(IC = I_D/I_{spec} = q^2 + q\), with \(I_{spec} = 2n\mu C_{ox}(W/L)V_T^2\). Weak below about 0.1, moderate 0.1–10, strong above 10.

column1: Write \(g_m/I_D\) in terms of the inversion coefficient. What are its limits?
column2: \(g_m/I_D = \dfrac{1}{nV_T}\cdot\dfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 + 4IC}}\). Maximum \(1/(nV_T)\) (about 30 V⁻¹ for n = 1.3) in weak inversion; about \(2/V_{ov}\) in strong inversion.

column1: Why is \(g_m/I_D\) a good design variable?
column2: It fixes the transistor's inversion level, so it sets efficiency (transconductance per current), \(f_T\), current density and \(V_{DS,sat}\) almost independently of width; width then scales current at fixed \(g_m/I_D\).

column1: What is a transistor's intrinsic gain and how do you raise it?
column2: \(A_i = g_mr_o = (g_m/I_D)V_A\), with \(V_A \approx V_A'L\). Raise it with longer channels or higher \(g_m/I_D\); both cost speed (\(f_T\) falls).

column1: Where does the product \((g_m/I_D)f_T\) peak, and why does that matter?
column2: In moderate inversion, for short channels: velocity saturation flattens \(f_T\) while \(g_m/I_D\) keeps falling, so the product has a maximum (without velocity saturation it rises monotonically). That region is the best compromise between power efficiency and speed for many analog blocks.

column1: How does velocity saturation change the picture at short channel lengths?
column2: It limits the current at high inversion (\(I_D \propto (q^2 + q)/(1 + \lambda_cq)\)), lowering \(g_m/I_D\) and capping \(f_T\) below the long-channel \(1/L^2\) law.

column1: Give the poles of a Miller-compensated two-stage op-amp.
column2: \(p_1 \approx 1/(g_{m6}R_1R_2C_c)\) and \(p_2 \approx g_{m6}C_c/[C_1C_L + C_c(C_1 + C_L)] \approx g_{m6}/C_L\); unity-gain frequency \(\omega_u = g_{m1}/C_c\). Compensation splits the poles.

column1: Where does the right-half-plane zero come from and how is it removed?
column2: From the feedforward path through \(C_c\): \(z = g_{m6}/C_c\). A nulling resistor \(R_z = 1/g_{m6}\) in series with \(C_c\) moves it to infinity; a larger \(R_z\) puts it in the left half plane.

column1: What bounds the non-dominant pole \(p_2\)?
column2: The output transistor's own capacitance: \(p_2 \le \omega_{T6}C_c/(C_L + C_c)\). Raising \(g_{m6}\) cannot push \(p_2\) past this.

column1: What sets the slew rate of a two-stage op-amp?
column2: \(\text{SR} = I_{SS}/C_c = 2\omega_u/(g_m/I_D)_1\); the output stage must also supply \(I_6 \ge I_{SS}(1 + C_L/C_c)\).

column1: Why does gain boosting create a slow-settling doublet?
column2: The boosting amplifier adds a pole-zero pair near its unity-gain frequency; if it falls below the main loop's \(\omega_u\beta\), a small error decays with that slow time constant.

column1: What does nested Miller compensation buy and cost?
column2: A third gain stage (more DC gain at low supply) at the cost of bandwidth: with Butterworth placement \(\omega_u = g_{m3}/(4C_L)\).

column1: Why does a bandgap reference work?
column2: \(V_{BE}\) falls with temperature (CTAT, about −2 mV/K) while \(\Delta V_{BE} = V_T\ln N\) rises (PTAT). Adding them in the right ratio cancels the first-order slope, leaving the magic voltage \(V_{g0} + (\eta - 1)V_T\) ≈ 1.25 V, a little above \(V_{g0}\) ≈ 1.2 V.

column1: What is the first-order compensated bandgap output?
column2: \(V_{REF}(T) = V_{g0} + (\eta - 1)V_T(T)[1 - \ln(T/T_c)]\): a parabola-like curve peaking at \(T_c\); the curvature is the floor of a first-order design.

column1: What does a one-temperature trim fix in a bandgap, and what can it worsen?
column2: PTAT-shaped errors (saturation-current spread, resistor-ratio mismatch) trim out at every temperature by adjusting the PTAT gain. A constant error such as op-amp offset is removed only at the trim temperature: the trim adds a slope. Curvature remains.

column1: Why does a β-multiplier or bandgap need a start-up circuit?
column2: The self-biased loop has a stable zero-current state; a start-up circuit injects current to leave it and then turns off.

column1: What is the box method for temperature coefficient?
column2: \(\text{TC} = (V_{max} - V_{min})/[V_{nom}(T_2 - T_1)]\) in ppm/K: it bounds the error but says nothing about the curve's shape.

column1: What is dropout in an LDO and what sets it?
column2: The minimum input-output difference at which the loop still regulates; set by the pass device's on-resistance (often in triode) times the load current.

column1: Why is an output-pole-dominant LDO hardest to stabilize at full load?
column2: Crossover \(\omega_c \approx A_{EA}\beta g_{mp}/C_L\) rises with \(g_{mp}\), i.e. with load current, toward the error amplifier's and gate's poles.

column1: How does an LDO's PSRR behave with frequency?
column2: Good at low frequency (divided by loop gain), worse near crossover where the loop gain falls, then set by the output capacitor and the pass device's coupling at high frequency.

column1: Estimate an LDO's load-step droop.
column2: \(\Delta V \approx \Delta I/(\omega_cC_L) + \Delta I\,R_{ESR}\): the capacitor carries the step until the loop responds.

column1: What is a capacitor-less LDO's trade-off?
column2: No large external capacitor, so the error amplifier must be fast and the output pole moves inside the loop; transient droop and stability depend on on-chip compensation and load capacitance.

column1: Why is kT/C noise independent of the switch resistance?
column2: A larger R makes more noise density (4kTR) but a smaller bandwidth (1/(4RC) noise bandwidth); the product is kT/C.

column1: What does a bootstrapped switch fix, and what remains?
column2: It holds \(V_{GS}\) constant so \(R_{on}\) does not vary with the signal; body effect still modulates \(V_{TH}\) and leaves some distortion.

column1: What SNR does sampling jitter allow for a full-scale sine?
column2: \(\text{SNR} = -20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)\): 100 fs at 1 GHz gives 64 dB.

column1: How does a latch resolve a small input, and what is metastability?
column2: Positive feedback grows the input as \(v_0e^{t/\tau}\), \(\tau \approx C/g_m\); inputs below \((V_L/A_0)e^{-T/\tau}\) (\(A_0\) = preamplifier gain) do not resolve in time T: metastability.

column1: What is the StrongARM comparator's integration gain?
column2: \(A_{int} = (g_m/I_D)V_{TH}\): the input pair integrates while the tail discharges the outputs by a threshold; noise \(\sigma_{in}^2 = (4\gamma/A_{int})kT/C\).

column1: What is kickback?
column2: Charge coupled from the comparator's regenerating nodes back to its input, disturbing the sampled voltage or the reference.

column1: What is the SQNR of an ideal N-bit quantizer?
column2: \(6.02N + 1.76\) dB for a full-scale sine.

column1: Define DNL and INL.
column2: DNL: each step's width relative to the average step, minus 1. INL: each transition's deviation from the straight line, in LSB; INL is the running sum of DNL.

column1: Why does a binary-weighted DAC or ADC have its worst DNL at mid-scale?
column2: At the MSB transition all the LSB elements switch off and the MSB on: σ(DNL) = \(\sigma_u\sqrt{2^N - 1}\).

column1: What are the Walden and Schreier figures of merit?
column2: Walden: \(P/(2^{ENOB}f_s)\), J per step (lower is better). Schreier: SNDR + \(10\log_{10}(BW/P)\), dB (higher is better); thermal limit about 192 dB.

column1: Why is coherent sampling used in FFT tests?
column2: An integer number of input cycles in the record puts all signal energy in one bin, so no window is needed; choosing the cycle count M odd with a power-of-two record makes M and the record length co-prime, so every sample has a different phase, and the noise and distortion are measured cleanly.

column1: What is the thermal limit on converter energy?
column2: \(P/f_s = 8kT\cdot\text{SNR}\) for an ideal class-B sampler: power quadruples per bit at high resolution.

column1: Compare flash, SAR and pipeline ADCs in one line each.
column2: Flash: \(2^N - 1\) comparators, one cycle, ≤ about 6 bits. SAR: one comparator, N cycles, mostly switches, very efficient. Pipeline: amplified residues stage by stage, fast and accurate but needs op-amps.

column1: How does a charge-redistribution SAR find each bit?
column2: The capacitor DAC subtracts trial fractions of \(V_{REF}\) from the sampled input; the comparator checks the sign of \(-v_{in} + V_{REF}\,\text{code}/2^N\), MSB first.

column1: What does redundancy (1.5-bit stages, sub-binary SAR) correct, and what not?
column2: It corrects comparator offsets and early decision errors within the margin; it does not correct interstage gain errors, which need calibration.

column1: What is the gain error of a flip-around MDAC with finite op-amp gain?
column2: \(1/(1 + A\beta)\) with \(\beta = C_f/(C_s + C_f + C_p)\).

column1: What spurs does two-channel interleaving create?
column2: Offset mismatch: a tone at \(f_s/2\). Gain mismatch α and timing skew Δt: an image at \(f_s/2 - f_{in}\), with power ratios \((\alpha/2)^2\) and \((\pi f_{in}\Delta t)^2\).

column1: Why can later pipeline stages use smaller capacitors?
column2: Their noise is divided by the gain ahead of them when referred to the input; halving C per stage gives total noise \(\to 2kT/C_1\).

column1: How much does SQNR improve per octave of oversampling for an L-th-order modulator?
column2: \(6L + 3\) dB (3 dB for oversampling alone).

column1: Why does a first-order sigma-delta's output average equal its input?
column2: The integrator stays bounded, so the running sum of input minus output stays bounded; their averages must match.

column1: What is Lee's rule?
column2: For a 1-bit higher-order modulator to stay stable, keep the NTF's peak gain \(\|\text{NTF}\|_\infty\) at or below about 2 (1.5 in practice).

column1: What is the drawback of MASH modulators?
column2: Cancelling the first stage's error needs the digital filters to match the analog integrators; leakage leaks unshaped noise.

column1: Why are continuous-time sigma-delta modulators sensitive to clock jitter?
column2: The NRZ feedback DAC's pulse width varies with jitter, adding an error proportional to the feedback steps; multi-bit feedback reduces it.

column1: What is excess loop delay?
column2: Delay in the quantizer and DAC of a continuous-time loop that changes its effective NTF; it is compensated with an extra direct feedback path.

column1: Why is a resistor-string DAC monotonic?
column2: Each code taps a higher point on the same string, so the output can only rise with the code, whatever the resistor mismatch.

column1: Why segment a current-steering DAC?
column2: Unary (thermometer) MSBs cut DNL and glitches; binary LSBs keep the element count manageable: σ(DNL) ≈ \(\sigma_u\sqrt{2^{B+1} - 1}\).

column1: What yield rule sets a unary DAC's unit-current matching?
column2: INL is a random walk pinned at both ends (a Brownian bridge); 99.7% yield for |INL| ≤ ½ LSB needs \(\sigma_u \le 0.5/(1.818\sqrt{N_t})\).

column1: Why do current-steering DACs need high output impedance?
column2: Finite unit impedance compresses the output with code: INL ≈ \(xN_t^2/4\), HD2 ≈ \(xN_t/4\); differential outputs cancel HD2.

column1: Compare NRZ, RZ and mixed-mode DAC outputs.
column2: NRZ: sinc droop, 3.92 dB at \(f_s/2\). RZ: half the signal but flatter. Mixed mode: zero at DC, peaks in the second Nyquist zone for RF synthesis.

column1: What does data-weighted averaging do?
column2: Rotates through the unit elements so each is used equally; the mismatch error becomes first-order shaped noise, pushed out of band.

column1: Write the open-loop gain of a charge-pump PLL.
column2: \(G(s) = (I_{cp}/2\pi)Z(s)(K_{VCO}/s)/N\): the VCO is an integrator in phase.

column1: Why does a charge-pump PLL's loop filter need a resistor?
column2: Capacitor plus VCO are two integrators (−180°); the resistor adds a zero that creates phase margin.

column1: How is the third-order loop filter designed for phase margin?
column2: Choose spread \(b = 1 + C_1/C_2\): \(\text{PM} = \arctan[(b - 1)/(2\sqrt b)]\) (b = 10 gives 54.9°), zero at \(\omega_c/\sqrt b\), pole at \(\omega_c\sqrt b\).

column1: How do reference and VCO noise reach a PLL's output?
column2: Reference noise through \(NG/(1 + G)\): ×N in band (+20 log N dB), low-pass. VCO noise through \(1/(1 + G)\): suppressed in band, high-pass.

column1: How do you get rms jitter from phase noise?
column2: \(\sigma_t = \sqrt{2\int\mathcal L(f)df}/(2\pi f_0)\), integrated over the stated band; the 2 counts both sidebands.

column1: Why do fractional-N PLLs use higher-order ΔΣ modulators, and what is the catch?
column2: To push divider quantization noise to high offsets where the loop filters it; simple rational fractions still produce periodic sequences and spurs.

column1: What limits an all-digital PLL's in-band noise?
column2: The TDC resolution: \(\mathcal L_{TDC} = (2\pi)^2(\Delta t_{res}f_0)^2/(12f_{ref})\).

column1: Define the PLL jitter-power figure of merit.
column2: \(10\log_{10}[(\sigma_t/1\text{ s})^2(P/1\text{ mW})]\): 100 fs at 10 mW is −250 dB; records are near −263 dB (as of Nov 2026).

column1: State Pelgrom's law and its design consequence.
column2: \(\sigma(\Delta V_T) = A_{VT}/\sqrt{WL}\): halving mismatch takes four times the area.

column1: Why do mirrors want low \(g_m/I_D\) and pairs high?
column2: A mirror converts \(\Delta V_T\) to current error through \(g_m/I_D\); a pair converts \(\Delta\beta/\beta\) to offset by dividing by \(g_m/I_D\).

column1: What does common-centroid (ABBA) placement cancel?
column2: Linear gradients (both devices have the same average position); a quadratic residual of \(2g_2p^2\) remains. ABBABAAB cancels linear and quadratic.

column1: What are layout-dependent effects, and how are they handled?
column2: Well proximity, diffusion length and isolation stress shift devices according to their surroundings; use identical surroundings, dummies, distance from well edges, and post-layout simulation.

column1: What is latch-up and how do guard rings prevent it?
column2: The CMOS parasitic PNPN thyristor turning on and shorting the supply; guard rings and taps collect injected carriers and lower the resistances that trigger it.

column1: How many failure-free Monte Carlo runs show a failure rate below p at 95% confidence?
What is Kinget's speed–accuracy–power limit?
column2: \(f(V/\sigma)^2/P \propto 1/(C_{ox}A_{VT}^2)\): each extra bit of mismatch-limited accuracy costs four times the power.

column1: Why is a corner simulation not enough?
column2: Corners model global variation only, not local mismatch, and different specifications are worst at different corners; Monte Carlo covers mismatch.

column1: Why does a noise-limited analog stage not benefit from a lower supply?
column2: For fixed SNR, \(C = 2kT\cdot\text{SNR}/A^2\) grows as the swing shrinks, and power \(\propto 1/V_{DD}\) at fixed bandwidth.

column1: What two things does a cascode cost at low supply?
column2: A \(V_{DS,sat}\) of headroom per device (swing ≈ \(V_{DD} - n_{stack}V_{DS,sat}\)) and an extra node.

column1: Which analog limits does scaling help, and which not?
column2: It helps speed (\(f_T\)) and mismatch per unit capacitance (\(C_{ox}A_{VT}^2 \propto t_{ox}\)); it does not help kT/C noise, and it hurts headroom and intrinsic gain.

column1: What is digitally assisted analog?
column2: Building imprecise analog and correcting it digitally: calibration, redundancy, dynamic element matching, digital PLLs. The calibration must estimate an error ε to \(\varepsilon_{max}/\varepsilon\) of itself.

column1: How much more capacitance does mismatch demand than noise for the same error?
column2: \(C_{mm}/C_n = C_{ox}A_{VT}^2/kT\): about 30 for 3.5 mV·µm and 10 fF/µm².
